rv.q: One of the dramatic highlights of the Broadway season.
This is a commanding illustration of the power of theater and a searing drama of morality and conscience that has as much to say to America now as it did in 1947.
What makes this revival so compelling is the way it demonstrates that Miller's examination of moral bankruptcy in the aftermath of World War II has lost none of its sting.
Letts' performance likely will strike some as odd or disconnected — I find it perfectly in tune with the moment.
Here, there is a disconnect between the staging and the play, when the one would ideally be illuminating the other.
Mostly this vaunting interpretation falls into that same limbo between intention and execution where so many of Miller’s baffled American souls find themselves.

Thanks to a stellar cast headed by Dianne Wiest, Katie Holmes and John Lithgow, this revival of Arthur Miller's 1947 drama proves both emotionally devastating and entirely relevant to our current economic crisis.
But this cast breathes so much life into Miller’s characters it feels like you’re watching for the first time.
Indeed, this mesmerizing production, makes its points simply by letting Miller’s words ring loud and clear – and in the mouths of some of America’s finest actors.
I did not see a moment that was not perfectly rendered.
It’s the performance that makes this production worth seeing.
